questions.question: Which of the following best captures the primary functional difference between an embedded system and a general‑purpose computing system as described in the context?

options.A: Embedded systems are designed for one or few dedicated tasks, while general‑purpose systems can run many unrelated applications.
options.B: Embedded systems always require real‑time operation, whereas general‑purpose systems never do.
options.C: Embedded systems use microcontrollers, while general‑purpose systems use microprocessors exclusively.
options.D: Embedded systems are always portable, while general‑purpose systems are fixed installations.

questions.explanation:
The context states that an embedded system has a dedicated/specific function designed for one or a few tasks, unlike general‑purpose computers which can run multiple unrelated applications [Page 10].

---

questions.question: According to the provided material, which characteristic would NOT typically be used to define an embedded system?

options.A: Tight hardware‑software integration with firmware stored in ROM/flash.
options.B: Being part of a larger device such as a car or appliance.
options.C: Ability to execute a wide variety of user‑installed software packages.
options.D: Performing a dedicated function rather than a general one.

questions.explanation:
The context emphasizes that embedded systems are dedicated, part of larger devices, and have tightly integrated firmware, not the ability to run many user‑installed programs like a general‑purpose system [Page 10].

---

questions.question: A thermostat controls heating based on temperature readings, stores its control algorithm in flash memory, and cannot run a word processor. Based on the criteria in the text, this device should be classified as:

options.A: General‑purpose computing system because it contains a microcontroller.
options.B: Embedded system because it has a dedicated function and tight hardware‑software integration.
options.C: General‑purpose system because it could be reprogrammed to run other tasks.
options.D: Embedded system only if it operates in real‑time, which is not stated.

questions.explanation:
The device matches the embedded system traits: dedicated function, part of a larger system, and firmware stored in ROM/flash, as described on page 10.

---

questions.question: Why is it hard to give a single precise definition of “embedded system” according to the context?

options.A: Because the term is used interchangeably with “microcontroller.”
options.B: Because embedded systems can vary widely in function, integration level, and real‑time requirements.
options.C: Because all embedded systems are also general‑purpose computers.
options.D: Because the hardware of embedded systems is always identical.

questions.explanation:
The text notes that embedded systems differ in dedicated function, integration, and real‑time needs, making a single definition difficult [Page 10].

---

questions.question: Which statement correctly differentiates an MPU (Microprocessor Unit) from an MCU (Microcontroller Unit) in the context of embedded versus general‑purpose systems?

options.A: An MPU includes CPU, memory, and I/O on one chip, making it ideal for embedded use.
options.B: An MCU contains only a CPU and requires external memory, typical of general‑purpose designs.
options.C: An MPU is a CPU only and needs external memory, often used in general‑purpose computers, while an MCU integrates CPU, memory, and I/O on one chip, common in embedded designs.
options.D: An MCU is always faster than an MPU, regardless of application.

questions.explanation:
Page 43 defines MPU as CPU only needing external memory and MCU as CPU + memory + I/O on one chip, aligning MPU with general‑purpose and MCU with embedded systems.

---

questions.question: In the activity description (page 36), which design decision most strongly pushes a system toward being classified as “embedded”?

options.A: Selecting a high‑performance desktop CPU for processing.
options.B: Using a microcontroller with integrated I/O for sensor data handling.
options.C: Allowing the user to install arbitrary operating systems.
options.D: Designing the system to support multitasking of unrelated applications.

questions.explanation:
The activity emphasizes identifying inputs, a processing unit (e.g., Arduino), and outputs—typical of an embedded design that uses a microcontroller with integrated I/O [Page 36].

---

questions.question: Which benchmark or consortium mentioned is specifically associated with evaluating embedded system performance?

options.D: Both A and C equally focus on embedded systems.

questions.explanation:
Page 100 lists EEMBC as “The Gold Standard for specialized chips (Car, Phone, IoT)”, indicating its focus on embedded systems, whereas SPEC targets desktops and servers.

questions.question: The text (page 105) describes a general‑purpose processor (GPP) as a “programmable single‑purpose processor.” Which implication best explains this description?

options.A: A GPP can only execute one program ever written for it.
options.B: A GPP’s hardware is fixed for one task, but its software can be changed to perform many tasks.
options.C: A GPP is identical to an MCU in every way.
options.D: A GPP cannot be reprogrammed after manufacturing.

questions.explanation:
The passage states that a GPP is essentially a programmable single‑purpose processor—it executes a sequence of instructions stored in program memory, meaning the hardware is general but the software determines the task [Page 105].

---

questions.question: When evaluating whether a system requires real‑time behavior, which factor from the context should be considered first?

options.A: Whether the system uses a microcontroller (MCU) or microprocessor (MPU).
options.B: Whether the system performs a dedicated function within a larger device.
options.C: Whether the system’s software is stored in ROM/flash.
options.D: Whether the system must meet timing constraints for its primary function.

questions.explanation:
Real‑time requirement depends on the need to meet timing constraints for the system’s primary function, as implied by the discussion of dedicated functions and real‑time behavior in embedded contexts [Page 10].

---

questions.question: Given the feature comparison table (page 13), which attribute most clearly separates an embedded system from a general‑purpose computing system?

options.A: The presence of a graphical user interface.
options.B: Tight integration of hardware and software with firmware stored in non‑volatile memory.
options.C: Ability to connect to the internet.
options.D: Use of a high‑speed bus architecture.

questions.explanation:
The table highlights that embedded systems have tight hardware‑software integration and firmware in ROM/flash, distinguishing them from general‑purpose systems [Page 13].

questions.question: A device can be reprogrammed by the end user to add new applications, but its hardware is optimized for a single control loop and is mounted inside a washing machine. According to the context, how should this device be classified?

options.A: Pure general‑purpose system because it is user‑programmable.
options.B: Pure embedded system because its hardware is optimized for a dedicated function.
options.C: A hybrid system that exhibits both embedded and general‑purpose characteristics.
options.D: Neither, because it does not meet any definition provided.

questions.explanation: The context notes that defining embedded systems is difficult due to overlapping traits; this device has dedicated hardware (embedded) but is user‑reprogrammable (general‑purpose), illustrating a hybrid classification [Page 10].
